Share of the evidence each study and design contributes

Source: R/diagnostics.R
information_share.Rd

Which studies the pooled effect is actually resting on, which a table of estimates never shows. Two columns, answering two different questions:

  • info_loss is the fraction of the precision of \(\mu_\theta\) lost by dropping that study, from the information matrix over \((\mu_\beta, \mu_\gamma, \mu_\theta)\) under the fitted hierarchy. It does not sum to one.

  • weight_naive is the inverse-variance weight, \(w_i \propto 1/(s_i^2 + \tau_\theta^2)\), which is what a conventional meta-analysis of the same point estimates would use. It does sum to one.

Usage

information_share(fit)

Arguments

fit

A meta_did() fit with summary-level studies.

Value

A data frame with one row per study: study_id, design, se, info_loss (not summing to one; NA outside the linear-Gaussian case) and weight_naive (summing to one), ordered by decreasing info_loss.

Details

info_loss sums to one only when no design enables another – a DiD-only fit, where it reduces to a partition of the evidence (verified in test-sensitivity.R). In a mixed analysis it sums to more than one, because dropping a DiD study also costs the pre-post studies the trend information they borrow from it. That excess is the point: on a 10/10/10 mixed fit the losses were 0.73 for the DiD arm, 0.19 for pre-post and 0.09 for post-only, summing to 1.01 – the DiD studies are close to indispensable, and not because they carry most of the weight on the mean.

For a design-level share, which does partition, use omega_pp(). The two are not interchangeable: on that same fit it puts the pre-post share at 0.414 against a naive 0.410. Note also that the obvious fix to the naive weight – adding \(\tau_\beta^2\) or \(\tau_\gamma^2\) to those designs' denominators – over-corrects, giving 0.367, because those designs help to estimate the nuisance means rather than only consuming them.

Both columns concern the mean. Neither says anything about a study's effect on the between-study SD, and a study carrying the smallest weight in an analysis can still double the width of the pooled interval – see study_influence().

\(s_i\) is the design-appropriate sampling SD: the double-difference SE for DiD, the change-score SE for pre-post, the ratio SE for post-only. Variance components are taken at their posterior medians. info_loss needs the linear-Gaussian case (summary data, baseline normalisation) and is NA outside it.

See also
